title: The King Comes to Jerusalem
summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey while the crowds hail him as the Son of David, then drives the traders out of the temple courts and heals the blind and the lame there. The next morning he curses a barren fig tree, and when the temple authorities challenge his authority he answers with a question about John the Baptist and two parables that indict the leaders who have refused God's messengers.
story: Since Peter's confession in chapter 16, Jesus has been walking toward Jerusalem and telling his disciples that he will suffer, die, and rise there. Now he arrives, and the final week of his earthly life begins. Everything in Matthew 21 to 28 happens in or near the city within a few days. This chapter is a public claim: Jesus enters as a king, acts with authority in God's house, and tells the leaders of Israel that they have rejected the prophets and are about to reject the Son. The conflict that has been building since Galilee now moves to its center, the temple, and the plot against him sharpens from here to his arrest in chapter 26.
historical:
The setting is the days before Passover, probably around AD 30 or 33, when pilgrims from across the Jewish world filled Jerusalem and camped in villages like Bethphage and Bethany on the slopes of the Mount of Olives, east of the city. Judea was ruled directly by a Roman governor, Pontius Pilate, who normally lived in Caesarea on the coast but came up to Jerusalem at festivals with troops, because crowds celebrating Israel's liberation from Egypt could turn restless under foreign rule. Day-to-day authority in the temple belonged to the high priest (Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36) and the chief priests, the leading priestly families who answered to Rome for keeping order.

The temple itself had been rebuilt on a magnificent scale by Herod the Great, beginning around 20 BC, and the work was still being finished. Its outer court, open to Gentiles, held the trade that made worship possible: animals and birds for sacrifice, and tables where money changers exchanged pilgrims' coins for the currency accepted for the annual temple tax. Doves were the offering allowed to the poor (Leviticus 12:8 permits two turtledoves or two young pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb). None of this was illegal in itself, which is why Jesus' action was read as a claim to authority over the temple rather than as a simple protest against cheating.
cultural:
Riding a donkey into the city was a deliberate sign. Pilgrims normally walked the last stretch into Jerusalem, and Matthew explains the act from Zechariah 9:9, where Zion's king comes humble and mounted on a donkey, not on a warhorse. Spreading cloaks on the road recalls the acclamation of Jehu as king in 2 Kings 9:13, and branches were part of Israel's festival celebrations. The crowd's words come from Psalm 118, a psalm sung at the great festivals: “Hosanna” was originally a Hebrew cry meaning roughly save now, which had become a shout of praise, and “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” welcomed pilgrims and the king to the temple.

The parables draw on ordinary rural life. Absentee landlords leased vineyards to tenant farmers and collected a share of the harvest through agents, and disputes between owners and tenants were common in Galilee. Hearers steeped in Scripture would also recognize Isaiah 5, where Israel is God's vineyard, planted, walled, and fitted with a tower and winepress, yet yielding only bad fruit. Jesus borrows the picture but shifts the blame from the vineyard to its tenants, the leaders entrusted with it.
literary: The chapter opens Matthew's long Jerusalem section (21 to 25) and is built as a sequence of symbolic acts followed by debate. The entry, the temple action, and the withered fig tree form a cluster of prophetic signs: the king arrives, inspects his house, and finds it fruitless. Then comes a formal challenge (verse 23) and Jesus' counter-question, followed by the first two of three parables of judgment (the two sons and the wicked tenants; the wedding banquet follows in chapter 22). Matthew weaves in Scripture throughout: Zechariah, Psalm 118, Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 in the temple, Psalm 8 on the children's praise, and Psalm 118 again at the chapter's climax, “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Readers should also notice that the leaders repeatedly condemn themselves with their own answers (verses 31 and 41).

outline.t: The humble king rides into Jerusalem
Jesus clears the temple courts and heals there
The fig tree withers: a sign and a lesson on faith
The parable of the two sons
The parable of the wicked tenants and the rejected stone

doctrines.note: Jesus publicly accepts the title Son of David and fulfills Zechariah's picture of Zion's king, but the king is gentle and comes on a donkey. His kingship is real and redefined at once: he rules as the one who will be rejected and killed.

The fig tree and the tenants' parable announce judgment on leaders who bear no fruit and reject God's messengers. The kingdom will be given to a people who produce its fruit (verse 43), a warning the chapter aims at religious insiders, not at outsiders.

The parable of the two sons defines obedience as a changed mind that leads to action. Tax collectors and prostitutes who repented at John's preaching are entering the kingdom ahead of respectable people who said yes and did nothing.

words.note: Praus, gentle or humble. The word Matthew uses in the Zechariah quotation (verse 5) is the same Jesus used of himself in 11:29, where he calls himself gentle and humble in heart, and it appears in the Beatitudes (5:5). It describes strength that does not force itself, and it defines the kind of king who enters the city.

Hosanna, a Greek spelling of a Hebrew or Aramaic phrase from Psalm 118:25 meaning save, please, or save now. By Jesus' day it had become a cry of praise at festivals. On the crowd's lips it is both a welcome and, without their knowing it, a prayer that Jesus will answer by dying.

Lestes, robber, a word that could also mean a violent rebel or bandit. It comes from Jeremiah 7:11, where the prophet accused Judah of treating the temple as a hideout, a den where robbers retreat after their crimes, trusting the building to protect them. Jesus' charge is not only about prices but about using worship as cover.

Exousia, authority or right to act. It is a central word in Matthew: Jesus teaches with authority (7:29), forgives sins with authority (9:6), and will claim all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). The leaders' question in verse 23 goes to the heart of the book.

christ: This chapter shows Jesus as Israel's king, the Lord of the temple, and the Son sent last of all. The entry fulfills Zechariah 9:9, and Matthew says so explicitly. In the parable of the tenants Jesus places himself after the prophets as the owner's son and heir, and predicts that he will be thrown out of the vineyard and killed, which happens outside Jerusalem's walls. Then he applies Psalm 118:22-23 to himself: the stone rejected by the builders becomes the cornerstone. The early church used the same psalm to speak of Jesus' death and resurrection (Acts 4:11, 1 Peter 2:7). The rejection that the leaders plan is the very means by which God makes Jesus the foundation of a new people.

hard.q: Why does Jesus curse a fig tree, and was it fair when it was not fruit season?
hard.a: Mark's account notes that it was not the season for figs, and readers have long found the act strange or petulant. Several things help. Fig trees in the region put out small early fruit along with their leaves in spring, so a tree in full leaf advertised something it did not have. More importantly, the Gospels present the act as an acted parable in the tradition of the prophets, who performed symbolic actions to announce God's word. In the Old Testament the fig tree is a familiar picture of Israel, and fruitlessness a picture of judgment (Jeremiah 8:13, Micah 7:1). Placed right after the temple scene, the withered tree signals judgment on a religious center that looked flourishing but gave God no fruit. Matthew then turns the sign toward the disciples as a lesson in faith and prayer. The act is about the temple and its leaders, not about Jesus' temper toward a plant.

questions: The crowds in verse 9 praise Jesus, and within days a crowd will call for his crucifixion. What kind of king were they hoping for, and what kind do you hope for?
Which son in the parable of verses 28 to 32 do you resemble more, the one who says no and then obeys, or the one who says yes and does nothing?
Jesus found leaves and no fruit. Where might religious activity in your life or church look healthy while producing little of what God is looking for?
